title: Walking between sittings
hook: slow walking meditation between periods of zazen

segments.voice: Yesterday: dokusan, the private meeting with the teacher, and your line, face to face. Did you say one thing plainly to someone? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

The bell rings, and a period of zazen ends. Nobody heads for the door. Instead, everyone stands, turns, and begins to walk in a slow line around the hall. One foot. Then, much later, it seems, the other. Hands held together in front of the chest. Eyes lowered. Someone glancing through the window might think the whole room has slowed to half speed. In a way, it has. Knees that ached a moment ago get to stretch, and the sitting goes on, just upright and moving. Today's word: kinhin.
screen: `THE BELL ENDS THE SITTING.` → `NOBODY LEAVES.` → `A SLOW LINE AROUND THE HALL.`

segments.voice: First, what kinhin is for. It sits between periods of zazen. The body gets a rest from crossed legs, but the attention doesn't take a break. Kinhin is the same practice as sitting, carried into motion. Second, the form. The hands are held in a particular way, often one hand closed loosely and the other wrapped over it, resting at the chest. In many Soto halls, each breath carries the walker forward about half the length of a foot: step on the out-breath, pause, step again. It's slow enough that walking stops being travel and becomes something you can actually feel: heel, sole, toes, weight shifting. Third, the schools differ. In some Rinzai halls, kinhin is brisk, almost a quick march, and it can wake up a sleepy body in a hurry. Soto halls often keep it very slow. Neither is a mistake. Both are the hall moving together, in one line, at one pace, nobody passing anybody. Fourth, why it matters outside the hall. The walk from the cushion to the door is the first step of the walk home. Kinhin is the hinge: practice learning to walk. The point isn't to move strangely forever. It's to discover that attention can stand up with you, step out the door, and come along to the bus stop. And when the bell ends kinhin, everyone goes straight back to the cushion, the same attention sitting down again.
screen: `SITTING, CARRIED INTO MOTION.` · `HANDS AT THE CHEST, HALF A STEP.` · `SLOW IN ONE HALL, BRISK IN ANOTHER.` · `ATTENTION LEARNS TO STAND UP.` · then, large: `WALKING ZEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you have room to stand. Get up, and rest your hands loosely together in front of your chest. Breathe out and move one foot forward, about half its length. Feel the weight arrive. Breathe in, and pause. Breathe out, and take the next half step. If there's no space, or standing isn't easy, do it seated: lift and place one foot, then the other, with the breath. Later today, if you can, give it five full minutes. The bell holds the time.
Kinhin. Walking meditation between periods of zazen: slow in many halls, brisk in some, always the same attention, carried on foot. Today's word.
Your line: walking zen. Today, pick one short walk, the hallway or the last stretch to your door, and make it kinhin: feel each step land before the next. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: In Zen halls, kinhin follows each period of zazen: practitioners walk in a line around the room with hands held at the chest, slowly in many Soto communities and more briskly in some Rinzai ones, until a bell calls them back to sit.
